title: Why the expected "no" to #51 is hard: bounded least-preimage ratios would force infinitely many primes p with p−1 smooth over a fixed set — and in every smooth family we can compute, those primes are there
line: Take a finite set S of primes closed under p ↦ prime factors of p−1, and the totients a_K = φ(∏_{p∈S} p^K). Every prime in a preimage has p−1 dividing a_K, so it is in S or has p−1 S-smooth. If only finitely many of the latter existed, the K−1 copies of each p in a_K could not be absorbed, every p ∈ S would divide the least preimage, and ℓ(a_K)/a_K would reach ∏ p/(p−1). Read backwards: a bound below that product needs infinitely many S-smooth shifted primes (for S = {2} this is Carmichael's ℓ(2^k) = 2^(k+1)). Computed exactly, the least preimage of a_K is one to three such primes for every K we reached.
